judge_assessment.explanation: The count error is real and the judge's arithmetic is right. Class A is 52, 55, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66, 68, 70, 73, 76, 96 with mean 800/12 = 66.666...; the scores strictly below 66.67 are 52, 55, 58, 60, 62, 64 and 66 — seven, not ten. answer_key.pdf states it twice: problem 3's commentary, 'Ten of the twelve students scored below the mean. That is not an error — it is what a long right tail does', and problem 10's Class A paragraph, 'The mean of 66.67 sits above ten of the twelve scores, so quoting it as the typical score misdescribes the class'. The judge is also right that the claim is load-bearing rhetorically but not logically: right skew is already established by mean > median (66.67 > 65) and by the isolated 96, both of which are correct. I confirmed the judge's positive claims too — median 65, range 44, mean 66.67, Q1 59, Q3 71.5, IQR 12.5, Class B mean and median 71, range 22, IQR 12, histogram mode 20-29 and total 40, tail probability 7/40 are all correct, as is every study-guide try-it (median 17; IQR 25 - 13 = 12). Notably the same style of claim is CORRECT in study_guide.pdf skill 1 ('the mean would be 11.71, higher than six of the seven values' for 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 40), which shows this is an unchecked prose number rather than a misconception. Beyond the judge, the delivered answer key carries two printed defects nobody reported: the Quick Answers bank prints '5. —' for a VERIFIED compare entry (verify.json id 5, expected '>'), the same glyph problem 10 gets for genuinely manual work; and it prints '8. −9, 40' where problem 8(a)'s answer is the interval 20-29, because scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt() calls sympy.sympify('20-29') and gets Integer(-9). I reproduced both: sympify('>') raises SympifyError and falls back to '---', and sympy.latex(sympy.sympify('20-29')) returns '-9'.

strengths_to_preserve: The two dot-plot data sets are engineered so the pedagogy cannot be dodged: Class A (range 44, IQR 12.5) and Class B (range 22, IQR 12) have nearly identical middles and wildly different extremes, so problem 7(c) can put '44 vs 22' beside '12.5 vs 12' and force the student to say which measure describes the bulk of the data. The key's table of the four numbers, and the line 'A statistic that one observation out of twelve can double is describing that observation, not the class', is the sharpest sentence in the packet.

Problem 1's solution makes resistance concrete rather than definitional: 'the extreme score of 96 had no influence on this answer at all — it could have been 960 without moving the median', and problem 4 repeats the same test on Q3 ('computed from the 9th and 10th values, so the top two observations could be anything at all').

Problem 9's 'Watch for' names the exact off-by-one-bar mistake with its wrong value — 'including the 30-39 bar, which gives 16/40' — and verify.json id 3 declares its trap as data ({'expr': '(52+96)/2', 'value': 74}) so the midrange distractor printed in the key's Common wrong answers cannot drift from the checked value.

Problem 10's manual rubric is genuinely gradeable: it enumerates (i) shape named, (ii) choice, (iii) what goes wrong with the alternative, states that a student writing only 'Class A is skewed so use the median' has (i) and (ii) but not (iii), and explicitly refuses 'always use the median because it is safer' as the absence of the judgement being tested.

The worksheet directions pin down the quartile convention ('school method ... with the overall median excluded when the count is odd') and final_response.md repeats it with the reason, so a teacher whose calculator uses a different convention is not left to discover a mismatch.

root_causes.description: The false 'ten of the twelve' count is a prose assertion in the answer key that no part of the verification pipeline can see. verify.json checks the mean (66.67), the median (65) and the quartiles, but the key's explanatory sentences carry additional derived numbers — here a count of observations below the mean — that are typed by the author and never recomputed from the data array they describe. Because the claim is stated twice, in problem 3 and again in problem 10, a single unchecked sentence propagated.
evidence: answer_key.pdf problem 3: 'Ten of the twelve students scored below the mean.' Actual count below 800/12 = 66.67 is seven (52, 55, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66).
answer_key.pdf problem 10: 'The mean of 66.67 sits above ten of the twelve scores'.
verify.json id 3 declares only {'measure': 'mean', 'expected': 66.67, 'tol': 0.01}; no entry counts observations relative to the mean.
gate_log.txt reports the full chain passing and final_response.md says 'Fourteen checks cover problems 1 through 9', so nothing in the pipeline examined the sentence.

root_causes.description: scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt() passes every string expected through bare sympy.sympify(). Two of this case's expected values are not algebra: the compare relation '>' (id 5) raises SympifyError and falls back to '---', and the histogram interval label '20-29' (id 8, query max_key) sympifies SUCCESSFULLY to Integer(-9) and is typeset as −9. The first makes a verified answer indistinguishable from unverified manual work; the second prints a value that is simply wrong on the delivered artifact.
evidence: verify.json id 5: {'type': 'compare', 'values': ['66.67', '65'], 'order': 'relation', 'expected': '>'}; answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '5. —' beside problem 10's genuine manual '10. —'.
verify.json id 8: {'type': 'read_data', 'query': 'max_key', 'expected': '20-29'}; answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '8. −9, 40'.
Reproduced directly: sympy.sympify('>') raises SympifyError; sympy.latex(sympy.sympify('20-29')) == '-9'.
scripts/render_quick_answers.py _fmt(): 'return "$" + sympy.latex(sympy.sympify(v)) + "$"' with an except clause that only catches failures, never a successful parse of a non-answer string.

root_causes.description: Four printed response slots that ask for written interpretation carry no manual entry. Problems 5(b), 6(c), 7(c) and 8(c) each require a sentence — name the shape and say why, explain why mean and median agreed here but not for Class A, explain which spread measure tells the truth, describe the histogram's shape and predict the mean-median relation — and verify.json declares only id 10 as manual. final_response.md therefore reports one item for manual review when five printed slots need a human reader.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 6(c): 'Compare the two answers, then say what that agreement tells you about the shape of Class B — and why it happened here but not for Class A.' verify.json id 6 has two 'stats' entries only.
worksheet.pdf problem 7(c): 'Explain which measure is telling the truth about the bulk of the data, and why the other one disagrees.' verify.json id 7 has two 'stats' entries only.
worksheet.pdf problem 8(c): 'Describe the shape of this distribution in one sentence...' verify.json id 8 has two 'read_data' entries only.
final_response.md: 'Problem 10 is flagged for manual review.' — singular.

improvements.title: Recompute every derived number an answer-key sentence asserts about the data, not just the requested answers
improvements.proposed_change: Add a lightweight 'claim' entry type to scripts/verify.py so a sentence-level number in the key can be declared and recomputed from the same data array that draws the display — e.g. {type: 'claim', data: [...], expr: 'count(x < mean)', expected: 7} — and require one for any key sentence that states a count, a proportion or a comparison of counts. Pair it with a SKILL.md rule: if a sentence in the answer key contains a number that is not one of the problem's verified answers, either declare it as a claim entry or delete it, because unchecked supporting numbers are the class of error that survives a green gate. A cheap first cut is a lint that flags number words plus 'of the' ('ten of the twelve', 'six of the seven') in ak_*.tex and demands a matching claim entry.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with curr-446's Class A array and an answer-key source containing 'Ten of the twelve students scored below the mean'. The claim lint plus verify must exit non-zero reporting the recomputed count 7 against the asserted 10; correcting the sentence to 'Seven of the twelve' (or declaring {type: 'claim', expr: 'count(x < mean)', expected: 7}) makes it pass. The same fixture must leave study_guide.pdf's correct 'higher than six of the seven values' passing, so the test proves the check discriminates rather than merely firing on the phrase.
improvements.expected_impact: Eliminates the hard failure in this case and the class it belongs to: correct answers wrapped in wrong explanatory arithmetic, which currently passes every gate and lands in the teacher-facing document twice. Restores mathematical_correctness and answer_key_quality here without touching any of the material the judge found correct.
improvements.risk: Over-broad linting will fire on legitimate prose numbers ('row 3 of Pascal's triangle', 'about one worker in six'), so the rule needs to target quantified counts over the data set specifically, and authors need an explicit escape with a recorded justification or they will start deleting good explanatory sentences to get past the gate.

improvements.title: Render the verified compare relation for problem 5 instead of printing the manual-only em dash
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, branch on entry type before formatting: a 'compare' entry with order 'relation' must print its relation symbol (and ideally its operands, '66.67 > 65') rather than being routed through sympify. Reserve '---' exclusively for ids whose only entries are type 'manual', so the glyph carries one meaning — nobody checked this — and a grader can distinguish problem 5 from problem 10 at a glance.
improvements.regression_test: Feed render_quick_answers.py curr-446's verify.json and assert row 5 renders '66.67 > 65' (or at minimum '>') while row 10 still renders '---'. Today row 5 renders '---', so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The answer key stops reporting a machine-verified relation as unverified. On a sheet whose whole argument is 'mean > median means skewed right', the one row that states that relation is currently blank.
improvements.risk: Low. The only care needed is TeX-escaping '<' and '>' correctly in text mode so the bank still compiles.

improvements.title: Stop sympify turning the histogram interval label 20-29 into −9 in the Quick Answers bank
improvements.proposed_change: Give read_data/label-valued expecteds an explicit non-mathematical rendering path. In verify.json, mark such entries (e.g. 'answer_form': 'label' — implied already by query 'max_key' over a dict with string keys) and have _fmt() print the string verbatim through the existing _TEX_ESCAPES table instead of sympifying it. More generally, _fmt should only sympify when the entry declares a mathematical answer form; a string that matches a key of the entry's own data dict must never be evaluated. This is the sibling of the builtin-leak defect: same trusting sympify call, different remedy, because '20-29' returns a perfectly valid mathematical object and no non-mathematical-object guard will catch it.
improvements.regression_test: Unit test on _fmt/render_entry with curr-446's id 8 entries: assert the rendered row is '20--29, 40' (escaped interval label) and specifically assert it does not contain '-9'. Fails today, passes after the fix. Add a second case with expected '10-19' to confirm the fix is not a special case for one label.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a flatly wrong number from a delivered answer key. Any worksheet whose answers are bin labels, ranges, dates or ID codes is currently at risk of the same silent arithmetic collapse, and this is the only defect in the packet that a teacher would copy onto a whiteboard.
improvements.risk: Deciding when a string is a label rather than an expression needs a declared signal; guessing heuristically (does it contain a hyphen?) would break legitimate expected values like '2-x'. Tie it to the entry type and an explicit answer_form field rather than to the string's shape.

improvements.title: Flag problems 5(b), 6(c), 7(c) and 8(c) as manual items instead of reporting a single open response
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual entry for every printed slot whose stem asks for a description, comparison or explanation, and have the manual count in final_response.md be generated from verify.json rather than narrated. Here that turns one flagged item into five and makes the key's already-written grading notes for problems 5, 7 and 8 the acceptance criteria for declared manual entries rather than free-floating prose.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture with curr-446's verify.json and worksheet source: the gate must exit non-zero listing 5(b), 6(c), 7(c) and 8(c) as explanation slots with no manual entry. Adding manual entries with descs makes it pass and makes the generated manual count read five.
improvements.expected_impact: The teacher's grading plan matches the sheet. This worksheet's whole design is interpretive — the key itself says 'Grade problems 5, 7, 8 and 10 on whether the shape is named and used' — yet only problem 10 is declared open, so the artifact contradicts its own grading advice.
improvements.risk: Manual counts rise across the corpus, which can read as weaker verification; the final response should state total checks and total manual slots together so the increase is understood as honesty rather than regression.

case_summary: A well-designed statistics sheet whose numbers are right and whose prose is not. The three displays are engineered so that Class A and Class B share an IQR (12.5 vs 12) but not a range (44 vs 22), which lets problem 7 stage a genuine conflict between two spread measures, and problem 10's manual rubric is one of the better ones in the run. The REJECT is correct: the key twice asserts 'ten of the twelve' Class A scores lie below the mean of 66.67 when only seven do, an unchecked prose count in a document whose every requested answer was machine-verified. Two further printed defects went unreported by the judge and are both in scripts/render_quick_answers.py: the verified compare relation for problem 5 prints as '—', the same glyph as genuinely manual problem 10, and problem 8(a)'s interval answer 20-29 is sympified into the integer −9 and printed as '8. −9, 40'. A fourth finding is that four interpretive slots (5b, 6c, 7c, 8c) carry no manual entry, so the response reports one open item on a sheet whose own key says to grade four problems on their reasoning.
